accuracy.evidence: Checked against the English national curriculum Year 1 and Year 2 reading comprehension statement (check that the text makes sense as they read and correct inaccurate reading) and the spoken language requirement to ask relevant questions, Common Core RF.1.4c (use context to confirm or self-correct, rereading as necessary) and SL.1.3 (ask questions to clarify something not understood), Flavell's 1979 account of metacognitive monitoring and Markman's studies of children failing to notice gaps in instructions.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented failures of comprehension monitoring: reading on while meaning has broken down (keep reading fast prediction, race-on fix-up card), guessing at an instruction with an unknown word (the ball move is refused as a guess until Huh? is pressed), pretending to understand (Pretend I get it card, Mia mastery item) and reading confusion as being bad at reading (feeling-huh prediction, bad and broken challenge tags).

lab_distinct.evidence: flaghuh models noticing a breakdown in meaning: word chips where only the contradicting word counts, a follow-the-instruction room where a new word (beneath, hamper) must be asked about before the ball can be placed, and two-meaning words (bat, bark, glasses) resolved by rereading the sentence context. No other flagship lab is about detecting non-understanding, and it passed the 30 percent shingle gate against flagtrick, flagthink and every other lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: The child has to stop on the exact word where milk is kept hot or a dog says meow, so the huh feeling is tied to a specific mismatch. Guessing at beneath is refused while asking unlocks the meaning, so the child experiences that asking beats guessing, and the two-meaning pictures can only be solved by rereading the words around the tricky one.

predictions.evidence: Three locked predictions with tempting wrong options: keep reading fast versus stop and notice, guess and do something versus ask what it means, and feeling huh means I am not clever versus my brain found something to fix. Each is answered by the step's own outcome (sorting, the refused guess, the fix-ups) and echoed in the done message.

challenge_feedback.evidence: Five rotating challenge questions with nine tagged wrong-answer messages (fine, pretend, race, guess, hide, bad, broken, coat, put). Each names the slip, for example a guess can be wrong while asking tells you for sure, or coats are for cold days so hot is the huh word, rather than a bare try again.

readability.evidence: Family audience gates pass: kid paragraphs score about FK 0.1 with short sentences and words such as huh, stop, fix, read it again; adult paragraphs use the precise terms comprehension monitoring, metacognition, self-correct and fix-up strategies at about FK 8.5 against the 10.0 limit.

no_filler.evidence: Content gate passed with no filler phrases and explanation overlap under 12 percent against every lesson, including Noticing when something is tricky and Thinking Before Starting. Each adult paragraph gives research, curriculum statements, named mistakes or the lab's tasks; item explanations say why the answer is right.

mobile.evidence: Walkthrough passed on iPhone 13 and desktop. Screenshots at 390 px in both themes show the word chips wrapping onto three lines at a readable size, the four room places as large tiles, the two-meaning pictures side by side, and every action duplicated as a button below the canvas, including one button per word in the spot step.

accessibility.evidence: axe-core reports no WCAG 2.1 AA violations in light or dark theme. The canvas aria-label repeats each sentence or instruction as it is spoken, every drag or tap has a labelled button (for example The word fridge, Put the ball in the basket, Huh? Ask what a word means), and canvas text uses theme ink on pale or slate tiles.
